summary:
Article 629 of Ethiopia's 2004 Criminal Code criminalises same-sex conduct between men and between women. Enforcement is rare, but the provision underpins pervasive anti-LGBTIQ stigma, harassment and violence and drives near-total concealment of identity: individuals generally do not publicly identify as LGBTQI+, and activists report surveillance, entrapment and fear for their safety, with harassment and violence increasing toward the end of 2023.

No legal gender recognition mechanism exists. Neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway to changing legal sex is available, so trans men remain legally women and trans women legally men. A trans person in a relationship the law reads through birth-registered sex can therefore fall inside the prohibition on same-sex conduct.

Stakeholder submissions to Ethiopia's Universal Periodic Review document discrimination, violence, lack of police protection and stigma in services, and note that transgender people are particularly at risk given the criminalisation framework. Societal discrimination is reported nationwide in education, employment and healthcare, and being outed risks physical violence and ostracism.

On 10 August 2023 the government raided hospitality venues in Addis Ababa, shutting down guest houses and arresting managers; the Addis Ababa Peace and Security Administration Bureau announced measures against hotels, restaurants, guest houses and entertainment venues suspected of involvement in homosexual acts and called on the public to report such incidents. In August 2023 security forces cracked down on 'homosexuality' while non-state actors drove an online incitement wave ending in physical attacks; the House of Guramayle reported online harassment of self-identified gay, lesbian and transgender people, citing an 2 August video calling for gay men to be stabbed and a threat reading "We should find them and kill them."

ILGA World recorded police residential searches without warrants following neighbour complaints, physical abuse during detention, and a 2014 case in which a gay man was denied legal counsel and assaulted by other inmates, with no trial records found. In January 2021 police disclosed the sexual orientation of two people released from detention to their families, and one subsequently died by suicide.

In July 2021 German authorities ordered the deportation of a trans woman of Qatari origin holding Ethiopian citizenship. She testified that after someone discovered she was registered as male in her passport and attempted extortion, she was reported to Ethiopian authorities, held about a year in an Ethiopian men's prison and subjected to physical and sexual abuse by staff and inmates. German officials argued she would be safe because she could "pass" as cisgender, citing the absence of explicit laws regarding gender identity.

No hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covers gender identity, and there is no freedom from arbitrary arrest based on gender identity or expression. LGBTI organisations cannot register: Article 69 of the Charities and Societies Proclamation blocks registration of LGBTI groups as "contrary to public morality," though national LGBTI organisations exist despite the ban. Pride events are not allowed and participants are unprotected, and no workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections cover gender identity. Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition.

Christian and Muslim groups campaign for harsher penalties; the Orthodox Church declared its stance in June 2024. In March 2014 the Council of Ministers endorsed a bill that would have made homosexuality a "non-pardonable" offence, but the government later cancelled that bill, with a spokesman saying the current jail term was deemed sufficient.
tangentialFactors:
The F&M Global Barometers time series from 2011 to 2024 scores Ethiopia 'no' on every protection axis measured, indicating a stable rather than deteriorating or improving picture across that period.

Broader civic space restrictions shape the environment for LGBTIQ+ organising: US State Department reports for 2010 and 2011 document Charities and Societies Law restrictions on civil society, anti-terrorism prosecutions, and arrests of opposition figures. Internet censorship has limited LGBTQ organising, and in the early 2010s some Ethiopian media outlets, cooperating with the government, restricted discussion of "LGBTQ ideology" without enacting the policy into law.

A 2009 Lund University master's thesis reports that media and elite discourse constructs homophobia, that the church campaigns hatred, and that female homosexuality is simply overlooked in public discourse, while attitudes were shifting under globalisation.

The AIDS Resource Center in Addis Ababa reported that the majority of self-identified gay and lesbian callers, mostly male, requested help changing their behavior to avoid discrimination, with many gay men reporting anxiety, confusion, identity crises, depression, self-ostracism, religious conflict and suicide attempts. Organizers of the 2014 anti-gay rally and religious figures publicly blamed gay people for the rape of children and young men, and an anonymous LGBTQ activist told the AP in 2019 of wide misconceptions that gay people may be culpable for rising rape incidence, a climate that deters young people from seeking services.

Stigma and discrimination toward people living with HIV/AIDS affects residents' ability to receive an education, find employment and integrate into the community.
localsOnly:
Article 69 of the Charities and Societies Proclamation bars registration of LGBTI organisations as "contrary to public morality," though national LGBTI organisations operate despite the ban. The DANA Social Club, founded in 2013 by Beki Abiy, campaigns for transgender people's rights to sex reassignment surgery.

Pride events are not allowed and participants are unprotected. No workplace or fair-housing discrimination protections cover gender identity, and no hate-speech or hate-crime legislation covers gender identity.

Same-sex marriage has no legal recognition. No legal gender recognition mechanism exists: neither a surgical nor a psychiatric pathway to changing legal sex is available.

In early December 2011 Christian and Muslim religious leaders tried to derail a sexual health seminar targeted at men who have sex with men; the government intervened and the seminar went ahead at a different location.
outOfScopeNotes:
The maximum penalty under Article 629 is reported inconsistently across sources: stakeholder submissions to the Universal Periodic Review put it at one year with harsher terms available under aggravating provisions, while a 2009 study of the same code reports up to three years for male homosexuality. The two accounts have not been reconciled.

The inventory does not establish whether the August 2023 raids or the online incitement wave produced prosecutions, convictions or sentences, and no post-2023 enforcement data is available here.

The 2014 bill to make homosexuality a "non-pardonable" offence was cancelled; whether a comparable legislative proposal is currently before Ethiopia's lawmakers is not sourced.

Whether the trans woman deported from Germany in July 2021 was ultimately removed to Ethiopia, and her subsequent fate, is not documented in this inventory.

No figure in this inventory measures trans-specific violence against a general homicide baseline, so no comparative magnitude of risk can be stated.
